title: I've built a full roguelike deckbuilder with Claude + Gemini over the past month. Here's what worked and what didn't
author: OneCity7064
selftext:
I'm not a programmer. My background is hospitality and sales, and I started this as a "can I actually make a game?" experiment. A few months later, Crownfall is live on itch: a dark-fantasy roguelike deckbuilder with six heroes, three acts, minion armies, a meta-progression Keep, a daily challenge with a leaderboard, async PvP and now an illustrated story mode.

Free in the browser: https://crownfall.itch.io/crownfall-shards-of-the-realm

The stack:

Code: Claude. Everything is a single HTML file built from about half a megabyte of plain JavaScript, with no engine or framework. Claude writes the code, runs automated tests in a headless browser (one plays all 396 cards to check none of them break), takes screenshots and checks its own layout.

Art: Gemini. Around 156 character, enemy and minion sprites, plus about 20 full-screen scenes and story paintings.

Music: Suno.

Backend: Supabase for the leaderboard and PvP ghosts, and GoatCounter for anonymous analytics.

What worked:

Treating the AI like a developer I manage, not a vending machine. I set rules ("UK English", "don't change the phone layout", "ask before updating anything") and play-test everything myself. Most of my job is now QA and saying "no, that's not right".

A test page and a player page. Claude builds a version with a dev panel (skip to any boss, add gold and so on) so I can test quickly, and I only ship once I've played it myself.

Sprites on a flat green background. Gemini generates each character on solid #00FF00, and a script cuts it out with soft edges and colour despill. It's far more consistent than asking for transparency.

Reference images for story art. Attaching the hero's existing sprite to every prompt, plus a short written description of their outfit, keeps the same face and armour across all seven paintings.

Real player data. Analytics showed only about 50% of visitors started a run, so we redesigned the home screen to one big "Begin your first run" button, and it went to about 75%.

What didn't:

"Fixed" doesn't always mean fixed. A layout bug looked solved until a new background made it obvious. Now I ask for tests with a real run in progress, not empty screens.

Gemini's image drift. It added an extra child to one scene, drew nine crowns instead of seven shards, and once had a hooded stranger holding the crown in the hero's big ending. Generate two or three versions of everything.

Desktop vs mobile. Most of my players are on desktop, but I tested on my phone. A lot of recent work has been making desktop not look like a stretched phone.

Discoverability is harder than building. Making the game is the easy part now. Getting people to see it is the real challenge.

Happy to answer questions about the workflow, prompts or pipeline. Feedback on the game is very welcome too.

comments.author: KingofKingsofKingsof
comments.body:
Thanks for the tip about the green background. I didn't realise you could specify a specific colour.

I had a little go on the game. It was a little laggy on my phone. Not sure if that's my phone (probably, it's an oldish Moto g31(w).).  I haven't played enough to give proper feedback, but just a few bits of feedback:

The map confused me a little as the next location you can go is lit up almost exactly like the last place you have been so I kept trying to click the next location beyond that.  

Also, I didn't really appreciate how many cards I have and what my strategy should be - for example, does my health regenerate or does the 100 point last the whole game? Do cards disappear or do I have them the whole game?

 A smaller health and the gamble of picking up health might feel more rewarding.

replies.author: OneCity7064
replies.body:
Thanks so much for playing, and for taking the time to write this up. This is exactly the kind of feedback I need.

The lag: it might well be the phone, but I'd rather not assume. There's a lot of animation going on. If you try it again, Settings has Reduced motion and Fast animations, which should help on older phones. I'm going to look at performance on lower end devices too.

The map: really good catch. You're right that where you've been and where you can go next look far too similar. I'll make the next choices stand out properly.

Your questions:

Health carries over between fights, so the 100 lasts the whole run. You heal by resting at campfires (the fire icons on the map), from some events and items, and you get fully healed when you reach a new act. Choosing your route around campfires is a big part of the strategy.

Cards are yours for the whole run. Every fight you draw a hand from your full deck, and played cards go back in for the next fight. After fights you can add new cards, upgrade them at campfires, or pay the merchant to remove weak ones. A smaller, tighter deck is often stronger.

Clearly the game doesn't explain this well enough, which is useful to know, so I'll make it clearer in the first run.

Smaller health: I like that idea. Healing would feel like a real decision. I'll have a think about the balance.

Thanks again. If you do play more, I'd love to hear what you think.
